network.overall_strategy: Construct ten distinct precursor- or reagent-defined routes to racemic aspartate, sharing intermediates only where chemically justified. These are not ten independently established mechanisms: fumarate and maleate ammoniation belong to one reaction family, and discharge chemistry can overlap mechanistically with nitrile chemistry. The strongest demonstrated transformations are cyanoacetylene-to-aminonitrile chemistry, oxaloacetate reductive amination, and oxaloacetate-derived hydantoin hydrolysis. Oxaloacetate, hydroxylamine, pyridoxamine, and several organic acids remain explicitly supplied boundary feedstocks; their presence is not evidence of demonstrated synthesis from C1 molecules. Thus this is a complete graph of the specified candidate transformations, not a demonstrated end-to-end geochemical system. Reaction nodes may represent experimentally supported multistep transformations, as identified individually. All settings are anoxic, and incompatible conditions require separate reaction episodes. Organic acid/base pools are represented by neutral parent formulas, including aspartic acid for the aspartate target; proton accounting in iron reduction is explicit. Null environment_formed means an externally supplied species or formation in multiple environments. Stoichiometric coefficients are omitted as requested. No enantioselectivity is assumed.

molecules.common_name: Carbon dioxide; dissolved inorganic carbon reference

reactions.name: Discharge production of cyanoacetylene from methane and nitrogen

conditions.temperature: 300-350 K bulk gas; transient discharge channels are much hotter
conditions.other: Electrical discharge in a locally methane-rich, oxygen-free gas mixture; initially exclude ammonia and hydrogen sulfide. Prompt collection into a separate aqueous reservoir is required.

reactions.mechanism: A lumped plasma-radical transformation forms carbon-carbon and carbon-nitrogen bonds. Hydrogen represents the net dehydrogenation coproduct of the target-directed fraction, not a complete discharge-product inventory.
reactions.reasoning: Cyanoacetylene production by discharge through methane/nitrogen mixtures is reported by Sanchez, Ferris and Orgel (1966). Its supply is a major bottleneck: ammonia and hydrogen sulfide suppress accumulation, and aqueous survival is limited (Shapiro, 1999). A separated generation-and-capture setting is therefore required, but its geological implementation is unproven. No copper oxidative-coupling cycle is assumed without an identified oxidant.

reactions.name: Discharge production of hydrogen cyanide

conditions.temperature: 300-350 K bulk gas; transient high-energy discharge
conditions.other: Anoxic reducing gas followed by aqueous capture; a separate gas episode from ammonia-poor cyanoacetylene production.

reactions.mechanism: Electrical excitation and radical recombination give hydrogen cyanide through a multistep gas-phase network. The displayed reaction is a target-focused net transformation.
reactions.reasoning: Discharge-generated hydrogen cyanide supplies aqueous Strecker chemistry in Miller-type systems (Miller, 1953; Johnson et al., 2008). Efficient formation requires a locally reducing atmosphere rather than an assumed globally methane-rich early atmosphere. Separation from rxn_001 follows the cyanoacetylene compatibility critique of Shapiro (1999).

reactions.name: Cyanoacetylene conversion to the aspartate aminodinitrile

conditions.other: Slightly alkaline, concentrated aqueous reactants with staged cyanide and ammonia delivery; avoid prolonged cyanoacetylene storage in sulfide-rich water.

reactions.mechanism: Aqueous addition and Strecker-type chemistry convert cyanoacetylene into 2-aminosuccinonitrile. Water participates in intermediate hydration and condensation but cancels from the displayed net reaction.
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al. (2015) report approximately 25% 2-aminosuccinonitrile, with maleonitrile and a cyanohydrin as major competing products. This is a demonstrated target-relevant branch, not a selective conversion. Copper and hydrogen sulfide are not assigned as catalysts here because their roles in other parts of the cyanosulfidic network do not establish a requirement for this particular transformation.

reactions.name: Complete hydrolysis of 2-aminosuccinonitrile to aspartate
agents: Hydronium ions or hydroxide ions during a separate hydrolysis episode

conditions.pressure: Approximately 1 atm, or sufficient confinement to retain liquid water
conditions.other: Sequential hydrolysis after aminonitrile formation; residence time and pH must be established experimentally. Acidic hydrolysis produces ammonium, represented by the neutral ammonia reference.

reactions.mechanism: Both nitrile groups undergo hydration through amide-containing intermediates and ultimately become carboxyl groups. The amino substituent is retained.
reactions.reasoning: Cyanoacetylene chemistry yielding aspartic acid and asparagine was reported by Sanchez, Ferris and Orgel (1966), while Patel et al. (2015) establish the aminonitrile precursor. The provided review does not supply a validated complete-hydrolysis rate or yield at the proposed conditions. Therefore the environmental implementation is conditional, and the 25% precursor yield must not be reported as an aspartate yield.

reactions.name: Oxaloacetate reductive amination by reduced FeS-associated iron
agents: Electroreduced FeS_PERM mineral interface containing reactive Fe(0) domains

conditions.temperature: 298-323 K candidate cool-interface implementation; exact benchmark assay temperature is not specified in the supplied review
conditions.pressure: Ambient to elevated pressure in a confined mineral-water interface
conditions.other: Alkaline ammoniacal solution contacting freshly reduced material. Fe(0) is a consumed electron donor, not an indefinitely regenerating catalyst. Explicit protons represent buffer-supplied proton equivalents, not an acidic bulk solution.

reactions.mechanism: Oxaloacetate forms an imine/iminium pool with ammonia. Electron transfer from reduced iron and protonation produce aspartate; Fe(II) is the formal oxidation product, although it may remain mineral-associated.
reactions.reasoning: Kitadai et al. (2019) report 64% aspartate from supplied oxaloacetate using electroreduced FeS. The graph explicitly accounts for reducing equivalents rather than treating reduced FeS as a free energy source. The stated cool-interface deployment is a candidate, not a claim that the reported yield applies throughout this range. Oxaloacetate supply, mineral re-reduction and competition with malate formation remain unresolved. Rapid capture is essential given oxaloacetate decarboxylation measured by Wolfenden et al. (2011).

reactions.name: Hydrogen-driven nickel-catalysed reductive amination of oxaloacetate
agents: Ni(0) supported on silica/alumina, as an experimental model of a hydrogen-activating metal interface

conditions.other: Approximately pH 8; ammonium/ammonia supplied; reaction monitored over hours to days. Keep separate from strongly cyanide-rich solutions that could alter metal availability.

reactions.mechanism: Nickel activates hydrogen and transfers reducing equivalents to an oxaloacetate-derived imine/iminium intermediate.
reactions.reasoning: Kaur et al. (2024) demonstrate hydrogen-driven amino-acid formation under these general conditions. Crucially, aspartate in their oxaloacetate/glyoxylate network was only a trace product with Ni; approximately 5% was obtained with Pd. Neither the wider ketoacid yield range nor the low-ammonia pyruvate result establishes high-yield aspartate synthesis. Natural equivalence of the supported catalyst, oxaloacetate supply and competing hydroxy-acid formation remain limitations.

reactions.name: Capture of oxaloacetate as its hydroxylamine-derived oxime

conditions.other: Add hydroxylamine to an oxaloacetate-containing aliquot before reductive workup. Avoid assuming that the oxime accumulates quantitatively or can be stored.

reactions.mechanism: Hydroxylamine adds to the keto carbonyl, followed by dehydration to an oxime. Oxime geometry is unspecified.
reactions.reasoning: Muchowska et al. (2019) obtained aspartate after hydroxylamine/Fe(0) treatment of an iron-promoted precursor network. Resolving that treatment into oxime formation and reduction is a chemically justified mechanistic model, not evidence that the oxaloacetate oxime was isolated or quantified in that network. The isolated-step conditions are therefore speculative, and prebiotic hydroxylamine supply remains an additional dependency.

reactions.name: Iron-mediated reduction of oxaloacetate oxime to aspartate

conditions.other: Acidic iron-reduction episode, distinct from alkaline ammonia/FeS chemistry. The literature framework includes strongly acidic Fe(0) workups; competing hydrogen evolution consumes reductant.

reactions.mechanism: Reduction of the oxime C=N bond and cleavage of its N-O bond yield the amino acid. Iron oxidation supplies the required electrons.
reactions.reasoning: The combined hydroxylamine/Fe(0) route to aspartate is supported by Muchowska et al. (2019). This explicit oxime-reduction node is an inferred mechanistic subdivision, not a separately validated prebiotic protocol. Kitadai et al. (2019) discuss the incompatibility of strongly acidic iron chemistry with ammonia-based protocols; Kaur et al. (2024) note disruption of precursor-forming networks by hydroxylamine/Fe(0).

reactions.name: Pyridoxamine-to-oxaloacetate amino-group transfer
agents: Dissolved Cu(II) coordinating the transamination intermediates

conditions.other: Reported benchmark: approximately 10 mM oxaloacetate, 10 mM pyridoxamine, 1 mM Cu(II), 50 mM ammonium bicarbonate and pH 7.8. Requires a sulfide-poor microenvironment that retains available copper.

reactions.mechanism: Metal-assisted ketimine/aldimine interconversion transfers the amino group from pyridoxamine to oxaloacetate, producing pyridoxal and aspartate.
reactions.reasoning: Harrison et al. (2023) report approximately 3-5% aspartate under copper-assisted conditions, with extensive competition from oxaloacetate decarboxylation. Pyridoxamine is consumed stoichiometrically here; no unsupported catalytic regeneration is assumed. Its prebiotic origin and Cu(II) persistence in reducing, iron-rich environments are unresolved, so this is a conditional biomimetic route rather than a closed simple-feedstock synthesis.

reactions.name: Bucherer-Bergs trapping of oxaloacetate as an aspartate hydantoin

conditions.other: Cyanide plus an ammonia/carbonate source in a concentrated aqueous solution. Carbon dioxide represents the carbonate pool and decarboxylation product; its occurrence on both sides does not imply an elementary exchange reaction.

reactions.mechanism: A multistep cyanide/carbonate-dependent capture, cyclisation and decarboxylation sequence yields 5-(carboxymethyl)hydantoin. The node represents the overall Bucherer-Bergs transformation rather than direct conversion to an amino acid.
reactions.reasoning: Pulletikurti et al. (2022) report approximately 69% formation of the oxaloacetate-derived hydantoin at room temperature. Trapping offers an experimentally supported response to oxaloacetate instability. Nevertheless, simultaneous delivery of cyanide and oxaloacetate remains unproven geochemically. The displayed net reaction does not assign experimentally unverified atom-by-atom carbon provenance.

reactions.name: Hydantoin ring opening to N-carbamoylaspartate
agents: Aqueous acid-base species under the hydrolysis conditions

conditions.other: Warm the hydantoin-containing solution in a separate hydrolysis stage; no mineral catalyst is assumed.

reactions.mechanism: Hydrolytic opening of the hydantoin ring forms N-carbamoylaspartate.
reactions.reasoning: Pulletikurti et al. (2022) identify N-carbamoylaspartate in the hydantoin-to-aspartate pathway at approximately 80 degrees Celsius. The reported approximately 68% final aspartate yield applies to the overall conversion, not independently to this ring-opening step. Competing cyclisation into pyrimidine-related products prevents assuming quantitative delivery.

reactions.name: Hydrolytic decarbamoylation of N-carbamoylaspartate
agents: Aqueous acid-base species under the hydrolysis conditions

conditions.other: Continued aqueous hydrolysis after hydantoin opening; ammonia and inorganic carbon are released.

reactions.mechanism: Hydrolysis removes the carbamoyl substituent. Decomposition of the released carbamic-acid equivalent gives ammonia and carbon dioxide.
reactions.reasoning: The hydantoin/N-carbamoylaspartate sequence leading to approximately 68% aspartate is supported by Pulletikurti et al. (2022). This is a supported downstream release step, but it does not solve upstream oxaloacetate and cyanide supply. Dihydroorotate formation competes with delivery to free aspartate.

reactions.name: Glyoxylate-malonate-urea multicomponent synthesis of aspartate

conditions.temperature: Mild aqueous formation conditions; a 298-353 K implementation is provisional because the supplied review does not specify the full protocol
conditions.other: Concentrated glyoxylate, malonate and urea; formation and hydrolytic release are represented together. Exact pH, concentrations and residence times require the original experimental protocol.

reactions.mechanism: A lumped multicomponent condensation, carbon-skeleton rearrangement/decarboxylation and nitrogen-incorporation sequence produces aspartate through ureido/carbamoyl chemistry. The supplied evidence does not establish a unique sequence of molecular intermediates, so none is asserted here.
reactions.reasoning: Pulletikurti et al. (2022) report aspartate and dihydroorotate from glyoxylate, malonate and urea. This supports the product-level route, not a fully resolved elementary mechanism or a yield under the provisional conditions listed here. Ammonia and carbon dioxide express the balanced target-directed net release, not measured coproduct yields. The environmental supply and concentration of all three feedstocks remain open.

reactions.name: Direct ammonia addition to fumarate

conditions.pressure: Elevated pressure sufficient to retain liquid water and ammonia
conditions.other: Concentrated ammonium fumarate with excess ammonia in a confined fluid pocket. This is not a validated dilute-vent protocol.

reactions.mechanism: Aza-Michael addition of ammonia across the activated carbon-carbon double bond, followed by proton transfer, gives racemic aspartate.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative as a prebiotic implementation. Fumarate is a chemically reasonable, more persistent alternative to oxaloacetate, and fumarate occurs in metal-promoted precursor chemistry discussed by Muchowska et al. (2017, 2019). However, the supplied review could not verify the historical ammonium-fumarate synthesis quantitatively. Maleate industrial ammoniation provides only an analogy, not measured fumarate kinetics or yield. Addition may be too slow at plausible natural concentrations.

reactions.name: Direct ammonia addition to maleate

conditions.pressure: Elevated pressure sufficient to retain an aqueous ammonia-rich phase
conditions.other: Concentrated diammonium maleate and excess ammonia; industrial conditions are a chemical benchmark, not a reconstructed early-Earth environment.

reactions.mechanism: Thermal ammonia addition to the unsaturated dicarboxylate gives racemic aspartate, potentially with competing maleate-fumarate isomerisation.
reactions.reasoning: The chemical conversion is supported by industrial patent literature summarized in the supplied research, including US5756839A (1998), which cites earlier maleate ammoniation processes. No peer-reviewed prebiotic validation is supplied. Its geological deployment is therefore speculative because ammonia concentrations, residence times and precursor availability are unestablished. This is a distinct geometric-isomer entry route, not a separate reaction family from rxn_014.

reactions.name: Low-selectivity methane-ammonia discharge and aqueous-workup route

conditions.temperature: 300-370 K bulk gas-water system; transient hot electrical discharge
conditions.other: Anoxic methane/ammonia/water system with electrical energy, condensate collection and aqueous processing. Hydrogen may also be present initially. Hydrolytic analytical workup must not be mistaken for spontaneous release of free aspartate in a pool.

reactions.mechanism: An empirical multistep process involving discharge-generated cyanide, carbonyl compounds and aqueous amino-acid precursors. The displayed hydrogen closes the formal target-directed net balance; the many other discharge products are not represented as a complete inventory.
reactions.reasoning: Miller (1953) tentatively identified aspartate, and modern reanalyses establish broad amino-acid production in related archived discharge mixtures (Johnson et al., 2008; Parker et al., 2011). Aspartate is a minor product, with methane-run Asp/Gly ratios of order 0.006-0.01 in the supplied review. This endpoint-defined route is included as a low-selectivity alternative, not as proof of a unique mechanism independent of rxn_001-rxn_004. Locally reducing atmospheric conditions and a natural counterpart to any analytical hydrolysis remain uncertain.

pathways.name: Discharge-fed cyanoacetylene aminonitrile pathway
pathways.description: Separate discharge episodes supply cyanoacetylene and hydrogen cyanide. Their products converge with ammonia to form the aminodinitrile, followed by hydrolysis. The first two listed reactions are parallel prerequisites, not a serial conversion of one discharge product into the other.

pathways.name: Reduced-FeS-associated iron and ammonia capture
pathways.description: Supplied oxaloacetate is rapidly aminated using ammonia and reduced iron domains. This is a demonstrated oxaloacetate-to-aspartate transformation, conditional on precursor supply and regeneration or replenishment of the reduced material.

pathways.name: Hydrogen-nickel reductive amination
pathways.description: Supplied oxaloacetate reacts with ammonia and hydrogen over nickel. Hydrogen can be obtained from rxn_002, but coupling atmospheric hydrogen production to the pressurised assay requires collection and confinement and has not been demonstrated as one system.

pathways.name: Hydroxylamine capture followed by iron reduction
pathways.description: Oxaloacetate is captured as a proposed oxime intermediate and reduced by Fe(0). The combined product-level chemistry has experimental support; the explicit intermediate and isolated-step conditions are mechanistic assignments requiring verification.

pathways.name: Pyridoxamine-mediated transamination
pathways.description: Supplied pyridoxamine transfers nitrogen to supplied oxaloacetate with Cu(II) assistance. This low-yield, cofactor-dependent route does not establish a prebiotic source or recycling pathway for pyridoxamine.

pathways.name: Bucherer-Bergs hydantoin protection and release
pathways.description: Discharge-derived cyanide and supplied oxaloacetate converge with ammonia and inorganic carbon to form an aspartate hydantoin. Ring opening and decarbamoylation release aspartate. The complete environmental sequence remains conditional despite strong downstream experimental support.

pathways.name: Glyoxylate-malonate-urea assembly
pathways.description: Three supplied small organic feedstocks generate aspartate through a reported multicomponent transformation. The reaction is represented at product level because the supplied evidence does not resolve a unique intermediate sequence.

pathways.name: Fumarate ammoniation bypass
pathways.description: Ammonia addition to supplied fumarate bypasses unstable oxaloacetate. This is an explicitly under-tested prebiotic candidate, not a validated high-yield synthesis.

pathways.name: Maleate ammoniation entry
pathways.description: Ammonia addition to supplied maleate has industrial chemical precedent but an unvalidated geological implementation. This differs from P8 by the supplied alkene geometry and evidence base, not by reaction family.

pathways.name: Discharge-mixture inventory pathway
pathways.description: Methane, ammonia and water yield minor aspartate through electrical discharge and subsequent aqueous processing. This experimentally defined aggregate route may include nitrile chemistry related to P1 and must not be interpreted as a separately resolved molecular mechanism.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This is a chemically supported route with correctly identified aminodinitrile and target structures. Sanchez, Ferris and Orgel (1966) support discharge-derived cyanoacetylene chemistry, and Patel et al. (2015) report approximately 25% aminonitrile formation under slightly alkaline conditions. Separate discharge episodes are compatible with avoiding ammonia-mediated suppression of cyanoacetylene production. However, collection, staged reagent delivery, cyanoacetylene survival and complete nitrile hydrolysis are not operationally specified. All four reactions pass the supplied conservation check.
suggestions: Specify separate discharge gas compositions and a physically justified aqueous collection and reagent-delivery protocol that limits cyanoacetylene loss.
Attach the experimental pH, concentrations, reaction times and approximately 25% branch yield to rxn_003.
Define the temperature, pH and duration needed for complete hydrolysis in rxn_004, distinguishing aspartate from residual nitriles, amides and asparagine.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Oxaloacetate reductive amination is strongly supported, and the supplied iron/proton equation is balanceable. Kitadai et al. (2019) obtained approximately 64% aspartate using electrochemically reduced, Fe0-bearing FeS. The reaction name invokes that material, but the submitted specification identifies only Fe0 and does not establish the mineral phase or its preparation. Pure Fe0 also supports the transformation, with different selectivity. Supplied oxaloacetate is a valid boundary feedstock; its competing decarboxylation still requires kinetic treatment.
suggestions: Specify whether the reactive material is FeS_PERM or ordinary Fe0, and use evidence and yields appropriate to that material.
Provide pH, ammonia concentration, temperature and residence time; formal H+ bookkeeping does not establish the operating pH.
Resolve the reported mol_011 formula/InChI discrepancy using an unambiguous single Fe atom with charge +2. This metadata issue does not overturn the supplied balance result.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The stated two-step pathway is interpreted as rxn_002 supplying H2 to rxn_006; rxn_001 could alternatively supply H2. Nickel-catalysed reductive amination is supported by Kaur et al. (2024), but their mixed oxaloacetate/glyoxylate experiment produced only trace aspartate with Ni. That result neither excludes the isolated-substrate reaction nor establishes a high-yield Ni pathway. The catalyst formulation, hydrogen pressure and transfer from an HCN-producing discharge are unspecified.
suggestions: Define the H2 source and recovery process, including HCN removal before contact with Ni to avoid catalyst inhibition or poisoning.
Specify Ni oxidation state, support or mineral phase, and operating conditions; the cited study used conditions including 22 degrees C, pH 8 and 5 bar H2.
Use oxaloacetate-specific conversion and selectivity data rather than yields pooled across different ketoacids or catalysts.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Oxime formation followed by iron-mediated reduction is chemically plausible, and both equations conserve atoms and charge under the supplied check. Muchowska et al. (2019) support hydroxylamine/Fe0 conversion of a ketoacid network to amino acids, with oxaloacetate inferred from products. This supports the proposed chemistry without necessarily establishing the isolated oxaloacetate-oxime sequence as drawn. Hydroxylamine is explicitly supplied and is not itself a network defect. Formation and reduction conditions remain underspecified.
suggestions: Distinguish experimentally observed intermediates from the plausible oxime intermediate assigned mechanistically.
Specify oxime-formation conditions separately from the acidic iron-reduction episode, including times, transfer and product workup.
Correct the mol_011 representation discrepancy while retaining the checker's balanced Fe0-to-Fe2+ electron accounting.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The balanced pyridoxamine-to-pyridoxal amino-group transfer is chemically legitimate. However, Harrison et al. (2023) reported only approximately 0.026% aspartate without added metal under their tested conditions, compared with approximately 3-5% with Cu2+. No such catalyst or operating conditions are specified here. This is therefore a supported but potentially very low-yield route, not an invalid reaction. Supplied pyridoxamine is an acceptable stoichiometric donor and need not be regenerated for this pathway.
suggestions: Specify whether this is the metal-free or metal-assisted protocol and use its corresponding yield.
If invoking Cu2+-enhanced synthesis, identify its concentration and environmental availability, together with pH, temperature and reaction time.
Quantify oxaloacetate decarboxylation and alanine production rather than assuming amino-group transfer predominantly yields aspartate.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This is the strongest specified pathway because it identifies the experimentally supported hydantoin and N-carbamoylaspartate intermediates. Pulletikurti et al. (2022) support oxaloacetate trapping and staged hydrolysis giving approximately 68% aspartate. All reactions pass the conservation check; CO2 appearing on both sides of rxn_010 is not a balance violation. Remaining gaps concern HCN collection, the detailed lumped trapping mechanism, hydrolysis conditions and competition with dihydroorotate formation.
suggestions: Connect rxn_002 to an explicit aqueous HCN collection and dosing protocol for the supplied oxaloacetate.
Document the substeps and carbon bookkeeping represented by rxn_010, including the role of carbonate/CO2.
Specify the room-temperature trapping and subsequent heated hydrolysis protocol, including pH, times and competing dihydroorotate formation.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The supplied literature attributes glyoxylate-malonate-urea production of aspartate and dihydroorotate to Pulletikurti et al. (2022). The net equation is balanceable with two CO2 products. Representing an experimentally supported multistep transformation by one node is acceptable, but this node does not identify the demonstrated intermediate sequence or product-release conditions. Its supplied substrates are legitimate boundaries; the uncertainty concerns execution and selectivity rather than their molecular complexity.
suggestions: Attach the specific experimental protocol, substrate concentrations, pH, temperature, duration and aspartate yield.
Annotate any established carbamoylated intermediates and hydrolysis/workup steps without implying that the net equation is elementary.
Track dihydroorotate and other competing products when estimating aspartate recovery.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Ammonia addition to fumarate is atom-balanced and can furnish racemic aspartate. However, the supplied fumarate-specific evidence relies partly on an unverified historical report, and useful conversion at geochemically relevant ammonia concentrations is not established. A Hydrothermal label permits heating but does not specify the temperature, pressure, ammonia activity or residence time required. This remains a plausible candidate pathway rather than a well-demonstrated environmental synthesis.
suggestions: Provide a verified fumarate-specific primary reference and measured conversion, selectivity and kinetics.
Specify and test temperature, pH, ammonia concentration, pressure and residence time rather than transferring maleate industrial conditions without verification.
Measure competing products and aspartate stability during the heating episode.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Maleate ammoniation has stronger direct process evidence than the supplied fumarate case. Industrial literature, including US5756839A and its cited processes, supports DL-aspartate formation using heated ammonium maleate with excess ammonia under pressure. This establishes chemical feasibility but not performance in an unspecified hydrothermal fluid. The network appropriately treats maleate and fumarate ammoniation as the same reaction family; no mechanistic-independence credit or penalty is warranted.
suggestions: Specify temperature, pressure, ammonia activity and residence time, distinguishing laboratory or industrial conditions from an environmental extrapolation.
Benchmark against the reported approximately 110-145 degrees C process range and test conversion at the proposed concentrations.
Include possible maleate/fumarate isomerization and competing product formation in the mechanistic annotation.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Aspartate occurrence in methane/ammonia discharge mixtures is experimentally supported by classic work and later reanalyses, including Johnson et al. (2008). The balanced equation is acceptable as an idealized net product channel, not an elementary or selective methane-to-aspartate reaction. The network correctly acknowledges low selectivity and possible overlap with nitrile chemistry. Exact discharge conditions, collection and workup remain unspecified, and the product mixture cannot be represented quantitatively by this channel alone.
suggestions: Specify gas composition, discharge energy, aqueous trapping, temperature and workup conditions.
Distinguish free aspartate from material released only after hydrolysis, and report absolute yield alongside Asp/Gly ratios.

Use low-selectivity benchmarks appropriate to the selected experiment, approximately 0.006-0.01 Asp per glycine for relevant classic methane runs, without treating this pathway as mechanistically independent of P1.

evaluation.network_feedback: The network is structurally valid and chemically credible as a connected collection of candidate transformations from the declared boundary feedstocks. All 25 molecule nodes participate, molecule references are connected, and the authoritative check reports 9 reactions balanced as written and 7 balanceable with coefficients, with no conservation violations. The inferred discharge coefficients are not intrinsically implausible for net transformations. The reported mol_011 formula/InChI discrepancy requires correction but does not invalidate rxn_005 or rxn_008 under that check. Several routes genuinely support racemic aspartate production, particularly oxaloacetate reductive amination and hydantoin trapping/hydrolysis. The neutral aspartic-acid representation is acceptable for the stated target pool. Supplied oxaloacetate, hydroxylamine, pyridoxamine and organic acids are accepted boundaries; their lack of internal synthesis is not grounds for rejecting this declared scope. The principal weakness is environmental specification: Surface, Biochemical and Hydrothermal labels do not establish pH, temperature, pressure, concentrations, residence times, catalyst phases or workup. Separate episodes are permissible, but physical handoffs and kinetic survival remain to be documented, especially for cyanoacetylene, oxaloacetate and discharge-derived H2 delivered to Ni. Literature alignment is substantial, although reaction-level citations and quantitative treatment of known limitations are missing. Flagged reactions have evidence, metadata or implementation gaps, not atom/charge failures. Neither the number of pathways nor the number or order of environments contributes to this assessment. The complete network does not meet the 0.9 approval threshold.

formula_mismatches: mol_011 (Ferrous ion): stated formula Fe2+ disagrees with its InChI structure (stated minus InChI: Fe+1, charge 1 vs 2)
